answer.label: Unverified — credited to Bill Gates, never documented
answer.authorDates: Credited to Bill Gates (b. 1955), Microsoft co-founder
answer.sourceLine: No transcript, recording, interview or press report from November 1994 has ever been produced for this sentence, and it appears in none of Wikiquote ↗’s sourced sections for Gates. Its one standing citation is a Danish festschrift about research libraries — a second-hand mention in another language, not a record of the event.

source.excerpt: Personal computing will soon shift away from the desktop and notebook-sized machines that are common today to devices of all sizes that draw much of their power and information from advanced communications networks.
trail: November 1994 — Gates keynotes Fall COMDEX with a vision of networked devices; the Chicago Sun-Times report of 14 November 1994 quotes him on machines drawing power from “advanced communications networks,” and carries nothing resembling the famous line (Elon University ↗).
4 October 2010 — a Wikiquote editor posts the sentence on the talk page, saying only that it “has been seen in a book,” with a link to one Google Books page (Wikiquote talk page ↗).

The book — that Google Books volume is Kommunikation erstatter transport, a Danish festschrift on research libraries edited by Erland Kolding Nielsen and three colleagues and published in 2005 — not a 2009 work by Karl Krarup, as Wikiquote ↗ states (Google Books ↗).
3 May 2011 — Computerworld lists the line among premature predictions of tech failure while warning that “some debate now exists over whether he actually said them” (Computerworld ↗).
source.excerptNote: What a contemporaneous report of that COMDEX keynote actually quotes Gates saying — a Chicago Sun-Times piece dated 14 November 1994, archived by Elon University’s Imagining the Internet ↗. The famous dismissal appears in no transcript or report of the event that anyone has produced.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for a sentence with no identified speaker, no documented occasion and no authored work behind it. The materials quoted alongside it — a 1994 newspaper report, a 1995 Microsoft memo and a 2005 Danish festschrift — all remain the property of their publishers; they appear here only as the short excerpts needed to document the trail.

author.name: Bill Gates
author.heading: About Bill Gates
author.metaLine: b. 1955 · Microsoft co-founder, software developer and philanthropist
author.bio: Bill Gates co-founded Microsoft in 1975 and was running it through the years this remark is supposedly set in — the era of MS-DOS, Windows 95 and the proprietary Microsoft Network. He was genuinely late to the open Internet, and has said so himself: the Internet sat at “a fifth or sixth priority” until Microsoft realised it was moving faster than the company’s strategy assumed. That documented admission is what makes the sharper, undocumented version so easy to believe — and so hard to source.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source exists. The standard citation is Wikiquote’s Attributed section, which gives “Remarks at COMDEX (November 1994), attributed in Kommunikation erstatter transport (2009) by Karl Krarup et al.” The book of that title is Erland Kolding Nielsen, Niels Christian Nielsen, Steen Bille Larsen and Sofie Lene Bak, eds., Kommunikation erstatter transport: den digitale revolution i danske forskningsbiblioteker 1980–2005: festskrift til Karl Krarup (Museum Tusculanum Press, 2005). No transcript or contemporaneous report of the 1994 keynote containing the line has been produced.

misattribution.heading: A forecast with no forecaster
misattribution.intro: The line is always placed at COMDEX in November 1994 and never at a transcript. Every trail leads to the same single second-hand citation — and that citation does not survive being checked.

items.why: Gates did keynote Fall COMDEX that month, and the keynote is well documented — a Chicago Sun-Times report dated 14 November 1994 quotes him predicting that personal computing would shift to “devices of all sizes that draw much of their power and information from advanced communications networks” (Elon University, Imagining the Internet ↗). No transcript or report carrying the famous sentence has been produced.

Wikiquote’s Attributed entry cites “Kommunikation erstatter transport (2009) by Karl Krarup et al.” (Wikiquote ↗). The book of that title is a 774-page Danish volume on the digital revolution in Danish research libraries, edited by Erland Kolding Nielsen, Niels Christian Nielsen, Steen Bille Larsen and Sofie Lene Bak, published in 2005 — and Karl Krarup is the librarian it honours, not its author (Museum Tusculanum ↗).

The entry traces to a talk-page comment of 4 October 2010: “At comdex 1994, it is seen that he said ‘I see little commercial potential for the Internet for at least 10 years’, at least this has been seen in a book” — followed by a link to a single Google Books page (Wikiquote talk page ↗).
Wikiquote prints “for the next 10 years”; the aggregators print “for at least ten years” with no source at all (AZQuotes ↗). A sentence with a real source does not drift like that.

misattribution.truthLine: Best available verdict: unverified. Wikiquote keeps the line out of its sourced quotations, and Computerworld — one of the outlets that spread it — concedes that “some debate now exists over whether he actually said them” (Computerworld, 3 May 2011 ↗). What Gates is documented as saying about his own slowness is milder and later: the Internet was “a fifth or sixth priority” until it outran Microsoft’s strategy.

context.heading: Why this one gets repeated
lead: It is the respectable member of the family. The cruder versions credited to Gates — that the Internet was a passing fad, that Microsoft was simply not interested in it — are obvious enough to make people suspicious. This one sounds like a considered forecast: a specific claim, with a horizon attached, of exactly the kind an executive actually makes. That plausibility is doing all the work, because the evidence is not.

And Gates really was slow. The first edition of The Road Ahead, published on 24 November 1995 by Viking Penguin, was criticised for exactly this: a Seattle Times reviewer noted that the World Wide Web received “just four index citations” and was treated as a functional appendage of the Internet rather than its driving force, and the book was overhauled for a revised edition in October 1996 (Wikipedia ↗). A real lag exists in the record. This quotation is not part of it.
context.detailsSummary: What Gates is actually on the record saying
detailsBody: In his 1995 internal memo The Internet Tidal Wave, Gates wrote: “Now I assign the Internet the highest level of importance,” adding that it was “even more important than the arrival of the graphical user interface (GUI)” (National Constitution Center ↗).

Speaking at the University of Washington in 1998, he conceded the lateness in his own words: “Sometimes we do get taken by surprise. For example, when the Internet came along, we had it as a fifth or sixth priority… But there came a point when we realized it was happening faster and was a much deeper phenomenon than had been recognized in our strategy.” Wikiquote files that one among his sourced quotations, citing a CNET News report of 2 July 1998 (Wikiquote ↗).
context.pull: Now I assign the Internet the highest level of importance.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote files "I see little commercial potential for the internet for the next 10 years" in its Attributed section, citing "Remarks at COMDEX (November 1994), attributed in Kommunikation erstatter transport (2009) by Karl Krarup et al." It also carries, among sourced 1990s quotes, Gates saying the Internet was "a fifth or sixth priority", citing a CNET News report of 2 July 1998.

A Wikiquote talk-page comment dated 4 October 2010 states "At comdex 1994, it is seen that he said 'I see little commercial potential for the Internet for at least 10 years', at least this has been seen in a book" and links to a single Google Books page.

The Google Books volume linked from that talk-page comment is Kommunikation erstatter transport: den digitale revolution i danske forskningsbiblioteker 1980-2005: festskrift til Karl Krarup, edited by Erland Kolding Nielsen, Niels Christian Nielsen, Steen Bille Larsen and Sofie Lene Bak, Museum Tusculanum Press, 2005, 774 pages, in Danish.
The publisher's record confirms the title, the 2005 date, the 774-page extent, and that the volume is a festschrift dedicated to Karl Krarup rather than authored by him.

Computerworld's "6 premature predictions of tech failure" (JR Raphael, 3 May 2011) repeats the 1994 line and states "A couple of infamous Internet-bashing quotes have been attributed to Gates, though some debate now exists over whether he actually said them"; it also quotes Gates's 1998 remark that the Internet was "a fifth or sixth priority".

Elon University's Imagining the Internet archives a Chicago Sun-Times report dated 14 November 1994 on Gates's COMDEX keynote, quoting him: "Personal computing will soon shift away from the desktop and notebook-sized machines that are common today to devices of all sizes that draw much of their power and information from advanced communications networks."
Gates's 1995 memo The Internet Tidal Wave contains "Now I assign the Internet the highest level of importance" and "It is even more important than the arrival of the graphical user interface (GUI)."

The Road Ahead was first published 24 November 1995 by Viking Penguin; a Seattle Times reviewer noted the World Wide Web received "just four index citations" and was "treated as a functional appendage of the Internet"; a revised edition appeared in October 1996.
AZQuotes prints the variant wording "I see little commercial potential for the Internet for at least ten years" attributed to Bill Gates with no source or date given.
